registers.role: sample frame (exclusion of parents with comorbidities)

children exposed to parental cancer linked to non-exposed children by coarsened exact matching on age, gender, area of residence and parental characteristics measured one year before the cancer diagnosis

sample.universe: a population-based cohort of children born in Denmark from 1 January 1987 through 31 December 2000

selection_rules: children born in Denmark 1 January 1987 - 31 December 2000

sample.n_observations: SP-I (basic school GPA): 1,105,694 observations; SP-II (starting secondary education): 1,117,022; SP-III (finishing secondary education): 731,359. Falsification treatment sample: 146,305 observations of children born 1987-1995 of which 6,389 (4.4%) experience parental cancer.
sample.n_individuals: unique children: 364,366 (SP-I), 337,846 (SP-II), 231,891 (SP-III); exposed: 23,320 (2.1%) in SP-I, 28,398 (2.5%) in SP-II, 25,362 (3.5%) in SP-III

construction_notes: Parental cancer is first modelled as a binary measure (cancer/no cancer), then decomposed by severity using the cancer-specific 5-year prognosis: good (survival rate above 85%), intermediate (50-85%), poor (below 50%).
Relative survival rates are allowed to differ over time, adjusted every fifth year, to account for changes in treatment options.
A cancer exposed parent is categorised as dying if death occurred within the observation period (before the child was 15, 18 or 21 of age, for each outcome respectively).
Matching and control variables are measured one year before the cancer diagnosis (baseline) to account for any adjustment in household behaviour prior to diagnosis.
Area of residence is divided into four categories: urban, intermediate, rural and remote (Kristensen et al., 2006).
Regressions are weighted to normalise the variance in the distribution, because the control and treatment group sizes differ.
Standard errors are cluster-robust at family level, to account for duplicate controls and sibling dependence.
GPA is the mean of grades in the compulsory ninth grade subjects on the cardinal Danish seven-point scale (-3, 00, 02, 4, 7, 10, 12).

Robustness: excluding lung cancers (-2.5% sample), excluding all endogenous cancers (-70%), matching on each municipality (99 categories, -91%) or on groups of municipalities (13 categories, -63%), matching in the diagnosis year and two years before, nonparametric estimation, and no matching.

Falsification population exercise: samples of children with healthy parents randomly split into control and fakely treated, repeated 100 times; samples of 141,715 / 160,435 / 168,565 fakely treated and 6,719,100 / 6,310,728 / 3,772,923 controls for the three outcomes.

links.pointer_quote: We find robust negative (albeit small) effects of a parental health shock on children's basic school grades as well as their likelihood of starting and finishing secondary school, especially for poor prognosis cancers.

We find robust negative (albeit small) effects of a parental health shock on children's basic school grades as well as their likelihood of starting and finishing secondary school, especially for poor prognosis cancers.

claims.statement: Experiencing a parental cancer lowers the child's ninth grade basic school GPA by 0.040 points on average.

treatment.label: Parental cancer (binary cancer/no cancer): the parental health shock

definition.value: A dummy equal to one if the child belongs to the cancer group and zero for the CEM-matched control group. A parental health shock is defined as the first occurrence of a cancer in one parent, diagnosed after childbirth and no later than the year of the child's 15th birthday (basic school GPA), 18th birthday (starting secondary education) or 21st birthday (finishing secondary education). Benign and precancerous neoplasms and non-melanoma skin cancers are excluded; children whose parent's cancer was diagnosed at death are excluded, as are children affected at age 0.

timing.value: Diagnosis occurs after childbirth and before the outcome-specific age cut-off; matching and control variables are measured one year before the cancer diagnosis (baseline).

outcome.label: Basic school GPA (ninth grade final exam grade point average)

definition.value: Attained grade point average (GPA) of examination grades in compulsory subjects completed in ninth grade (around the age of 15-16) in Danish public and private schools; compulsory subjects are Danish (written and oral), mathematics (written) and English (oral). Grades are on the Danish seven-point numerical scale (-3, 00, 02, 4, 7, 10, 12). Study population I.

timing.value: Measured in ninth grade, around the age of 15-16 (grade registration exists from the school year 2001/2002)

units.value: GPA points on the Danish seven-point grading scale (-3, 00, 02, 4, 7, 10, 12)

magnitude.interpretation: constituting 0.6% of average GPA or equivalent to 0.018 standard deviations

estimand.target_population: Children in Denmark born 1987-2000 whose parent was diagnosed with a first cancer, relative to their coarsened-exact-matched controls (the matched treated population).
estimand.time_horizon: School outcome measured in ninth grade (around age 15-16); the parental cancer may be diagnosed at any point from after childbirth up to the year of the child's 15th birthday. The paper reports no event-time horizon.

population.description: Children born in Denmark 1 January 1987 - 31 December 2000 who sat the ninth-grade final exams: children whose parent was diagnosed with a first cancer after childbirth and no later than the year of the child's 15th birthday, together with CEM-matched control children with no parental cancer (study population I).
population.ages: outcome measured in ninth grade, around age 15-16
population.period: children born 1987-2000; school outcomes observed over the following school careers (ninth-grade grade registration was established from the school year 2001/2002)
subgroups_defined: shock strength: average effect of cancer, good prognosis (survival rate above 85%), intermediate prognosis (50-85%), poor prognosis (below 50%)
parental cancer survivors vs. parental cancer deaths
gender of the ill parent, and child-parent gender composition
child's gender and child's age at diagnosis (1-2, 3-5, 6-9, 10-12, 13-15, 16-18, 19-21)
family-related resilience factors: descendant of migrants, not living with both parents, no living grandparents, low educated parents, low family income
population.selection: Children born in Denmark 1987-2000 and linked to their parents by the personal identification number. Control children must have parents without comorbidities (Charlson comorbidity index) who do not die during the study period and who are not exposed to cancer up to the final year of follow-up; treated children must have a healthy parent who is alive and without comorbidities during the study period and an ill parent without comorbidities one year before the cancer diagnosis; children whose parent's cancer was diagnosed at death and children affected at age 0 are excluded. The ninth-grade GPA sample only includes children who attended the exams.

identification.source_of_variation: Onset (first diagnosis) of a cancer in one parent, argued to be unanticipated because the precise timing of the shock is random. Children exposed to parental cancer are coarsened-exact-matched, one year before the diagnosis, to children with no parental health shock on age, gender, area of residence and parental characteristics; severity is measured by cancer-specific 5-year statistical survival rates rather than by individual disease outcomes.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unconfoundedness / selection on observables: conditional on the coarsened-exact matching variables and the full set of control variables measured one year before the cancer diagnosis, which parent is diagnosed with a first cancer is independent of the children's potential school outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Balance after matching (standardised mean difference below 10%, Table A5); the falsification treatment exercise (cancer diagnosed at least 2.5 years after the exam); and the falsification population exercise, whose Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests reject that the base case estimates come from the simulated distributions (p values of 0.02).

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the first onset of a cancer is unanticipated because the precise timing of the shock is random, and household behaviour has not yet adjusted at the baseline measured one year before diagnosis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors match and measure control variables one year before the cancer diagnosis to account for any adjustment in household behaviour prior to diagnosis; the falsification treatment exercise uses a 2.5-year threshold for the same reason.

key_assumptions.assumption: Overlap: every child exposed to parental cancer has matching non-exposed children with the same coarsened age, gender, area of residence and parental characteristics; the differing group sizes are handled by weighting the regressions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Coarsened exact matching matches each exposed child to all children with similar characteristics, and the regressions are weighted to normalise the variance in the distribution.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on survivorship and health of the non-exposed parent and of control parents (no Charlson comorbidities, no death during the study period, cancer not diagnosed at death) and, for GPA, on the child having sat the ninth-grade exams; this selection is assumed not to distort the contrast.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The exclusion criteria are listed in Table A1; the authors note that the GPA results are likely an underestimation because the sample only includes children who attended the exams.

key_assumptions.assumption: Remaining unobserved parental characteristics (lifestyle, inherited ability, personal traits) that affect both cancer risk and investment in children cannot be controlled for perfectly, but the resulting bias is assumed to be small.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue the bias is small because they also match on area of residence and control for municipality, and because most lifestyle cancers do not present in the prime childbearing and parental age.

evidence.annotation: Fig. 1. The impact of shock strength. Note: The figure displays regression coefficients and their 95% confidence intervals (clustered at family level). We regress cancer on both basic school GPA and binary outcomes for commencement and completion of secondary school for each shock strength and robustness check. All specifications include the additional controls: gender (1 dummy), month of birth (12 dummies), year of birth (14, 12 or 9 dummies, respectively), birth weight (6 dummies), gestational weeks (6 dummies), mother and father's age at birth (10 dummies), birth order (3 dummies), number of siblings (4 dummies), parents' cohabiting status (4 dummies), municipality (99 dummies), non-Danish ethnicity (1 dummy), living grandparents (1 dummy), mother and father's occupation (12 dummies), mother and father's education (10 dummies), and family income (4 dummies).

definition.value: A dummy equal to one if the child belongs to the cancer group and zero for the CEM-matched control group. claims.statement: A father's cancer diagnosis has no apparent effect on sons' school achievements, in particular on completing secondary education.

treatment.label: Father diagnosed with cancer, son

definition.value: A dummy equal to one if the child belongs to the cancer group and zero for the CEM-matched control group. A parental health shock is defined as the first occurrence of a cancer in one parent, diagnosed after childbirth and no later than the year of the child's 15th birthday (basic school GPA), 18th birthday (starting secondary education) or 21st birthday (finishing secondary education). Benign and precancerous neoplasms and non-melanoma skin cancers are excluded; children whose parent's cancer was diagnosed at death are excluded, as are children affected at age 0. The cancer term is split by the ill parent's gender interacted with the child's gender; this is the coefficient for a paternal diagnosis among sons.

timing.value: Diagnosis occurs after childbirth and before the outcome-specific age cut-off; matching and control variables are measured one year before the cancer diagnosis (baseline).

definition.value: Binary indicator: a child is categorised as having finished secondary education if completed no later than the year of turning 21 years, regardless of whether they started or not. Study population III.

population.selection: Children born in Denmark 1987-2000 and linked to their parents by the personal identification number. Control children must have parents without comorbidities (Charlson comorbidity index) who do not die during the study period and who are not exposed to cancer up to the final year of follow-up; treated children must have a healthy parent who is alive and without comorbidities during the study period and an ill parent without comorbidities one year before the cancer diagnosis; children whose parent's cancer was diagnosed at death and children affected at age 0 are excluded. definition.value: A dummy equal to one if the child belongs to the cancer group and zero for the CEM-matched control group. definition.value: The coefficient beta2 on the interaction between the parental cancer dummy and a dummy for Low family income. timing.value: Diagnosis occurs after childbirth and before the outcome-specific age cut-off; matching and control variables are measured one year before the cancer diagnosis (baseline). The family-related characteristic is measured, like the other control and matching variables, one year before the cancer diagnosis.

definition.value: Binary indicator: a child is categorised as having finished secondary education if completed no later than the year of turning 21 years, regardless of whether they started or not. Study population III.

timing.value: Measured by the year of the child's 21st birthday

estimand.target_population: Children in Denmark born 1987-2000 whose parent was diagnosed with a first cancer and who have the family-related characteristic 'Low family income', relative to their matched controls.
estimand.time_horizon: School outcome measured by the year of the child's 21st birthday; the parental cancer may be diagnosed at any point from after childbirth up to that year. The paper reports no event-time horizon.

population.description: Children born in Denmark 1987-1995: children whose parent was diagnosed with a first cancer after childbirth and no later than the year of the child's 21st birthday, together with CEM-matched control children with no parental cancer (study population III).
population.ages: outcome measured by the year of the child's 21st birthday
population.period: children born 1987-1995; school outcomes observed over the following school careers (ninth-grade grade registration was established from the school year 2001/2002)
subgroups_defined: shock strength: average effect of cancer, good prognosis (survival rate above 85%), intermediate prognosis (50-85%), poor prognosis (below 50%)
parental cancer survivors vs. parental cancer deaths
gender of the ill parent, and child-parent gender composition

population.selection: Children born in Denmark 1987-2000 and linked to their parents by the personal identification number. Control children must have parents without comorbidities (Charlson comorbidity index) who do not die during the study period and who are not exposed to cancer up to the final year of follow-up; treated children must have a healthy parent who is alive and without comorbidities during the study period and an ill parent without comorbidities one year before the cancer diagnosis; children whose parent's cancer was diagnosed at death and children affected at age 0 are excluded. The ninth-grade GPA sample only includes children who attended the exams.

identification.source_of_variation: Onset (first diagnosis) of a cancer in one parent, argued to be unanticipated because the precise timing of the shock is random. Children exposed to parental cancer are coarsened-exact-matched, one year before the diagnosis, to children with no parental health shock on age, gender, area of residence and parental characteristics; severity is measured by cancer-specific 5-year statistical survival rates rather than by individual disease outcomes.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unconfoundedness / selection on observables: conditional on the coarsened-exact matching variables and the full set of control variables measured one year before the cancer diagnosis, which parent is diagnosed with a first cancer is independent of the children's potential school outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Balance after matching (standardised mean difference below 10%, Table A5); the falsification treatment exercise (cancer diagnosed at least 2.5 years after the exam); and the falsification population exercise, whose Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests reject that the base case estimates come from the simulated distributions (p values of 0.02).

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the first onset of a cancer is unanticipated because the precise timing of the shock is random, and household behaviour has not yet adjusted at the baseline measured one year before diagnosis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors match and measure control variables one year before the cancer diagnosis to account for any adjustment in household behaviour prior to diagnosis; the falsification treatment exercise uses a 2.5-year threshold for the same reason.

key_assumptions.assumption: Overlap: every child exposed to parental cancer has matching non-exposed children with the same coarsened age, gender, area of residence and parental characteristics; the differing group sizes are handled by weighting the regressions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Coarsened exact matching matches each exposed child to all children with similar characteristics, and the regressions are weighted to normalise the variance in the distribution.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on survivorship and health of the non-exposed parent and of control parents (no Charlson comorbidities, no death during the study period, cancer not diagnosed at death) and, for GPA, on the child having sat the ninth-grade exams; this selection is assumed not to distort the contrast.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The exclusion criteria are listed in Table A1; the authors note that the GPA results are likely an underestimation because the sample only includes children who attended the exams.

key_assumptions.assumption: Remaining unobserved parental characteristics (lifestyle, inherited ability, personal traits) that affect both cancer risk and investment in children cannot be controlled for perfectly, but the resulting bias is assumed to be small.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue the bias is small because they also match on area of residence and control for municipality, and because most lifestyle cancers do not present in the prime childbearing and parental age.
